Choose a topic (tap 1..5)

1) Why we approved a CAN driver that silently dropped frames under 80% bus load
Hook: I signed off on a CAN transmission function that returned success even when the hardware mailbox was full.
Why: CAN controllers have finite TX mailboxes and no standard API return semantics—approval assumed send-and-forget worked, but mailbox exhaustion caused silent message loss in production vehicles.

2) The volatile keyword won't save your memory-mapped register access from compiler reordering
Hook: Our peripheral init sequence worked for two years until a compiler update reordered our register writes and bricked 200 units.
Why: Volatile prevents elimination but not reordering—compiler barriers and hardware memory fences are required, yet most reviews never check the generated assembly for MMIO sequences.

3) Stack overflow detection that only triggers after corruption has already propagated
Hook: We debugged a watchdog reset for three weeks before realizing the stack overflow happened 40ms before the canary check ever ran.
Why: RTOS stack canaries and watermark checks run periodically or on context switch—by then, adjacent memory may already be corrupted, masking the true root cause during postmortem.

4) Why our bootloader bricked devices during power loss—despite passing every bench test
Hook: Our firmware update routine had a two-second window where power loss would corrupt both images, and our test rig never hit it.
Why: Flash write atomicity assumptions break across real-world power-down curves—bench testing with hard shutoffs misses capacitor discharge timing and partial page corruption modes seen in the field.

5) ISR execution time under 10 microseconds—until the peripheral asserted the interrupt again inside the handler
Hook: I approved an ISR that met timing budgets on the scope but starved the RTOS scheduler when the sensor data rate spiked.
Why: Interrupt re-entry or rapid reassertion can occur if the ISR clears flags before servicing the root cause—measured ISR timing in isolation hides cumulative starvation of lower-priority tasks.
